lead: A pass transistor connects an input to an output through a switch, so data flows without a logic gate. An nMOS alone cannot pass a full logic 1: it stops one threshold voltage below its gate. A pMOS alone cannot pass a full logic 0. A transmission gate puts an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel, with complementary controls, and passes both rails. These circuits are used in multiplexers, XOR gates, flip-flops and adder cells, where saving transistors matters more than restoring every node.
prereq: You need: threshold voltage and body effect from Unit 1, and static CMOS from Chapter 3.7.

sections.h3: nMOS pass transistor and threshold drop

blocks.text: An nMOS pass transistor is one nMOS switch placed between a data input A and an output Y. The gate is the control C. When C is high, the channel can connect A to Y. The switch is not a gate: it does not invert or restore the signal; it only passes it.

Passing a low input works well. With A = 0 V and C = V<sub>DD</sub>, the input side A is the source because it is at the lower potential. Then V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>G</sub> − V<sub>A</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − 0 V = V<sub>DD</sub>, independent of Y. The nMOS stays on for the whole discharge, so Y reaches 0 V. Use V<sub>GS</sub> = C − Y only for the high-level case, where the output Y is the source.

Passing a high input is different. Start with Y at 0 V and A = V<sub>DD</sub>. The nMOS turns on and charges Y. As Y rises, V<sub>GS</sub> falls because V<sub>GS</sub> = C − Y; here Y is the source. The transistor turns off when V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>tn</sub>, where V<sub>tn</sub> is the nMOS threshold voltage in V. At that point Y stops at V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>. The highest output is min(V<sub>in</sub>, V<sub>G</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>).

blocks.where: V<sub>out(max)</sub> is the highest output voltage in V; V<sub>in</sub> is the input high level in V; V<sub>G</sub> is the gate voltage in V; V<sub>tn</sub> is the nMOS threshold in V.

blocks.text: When Y is above ground, the source-to-body voltage V<sub>SB</sub> is not zero. The threshold rises with body effect:

blocks.where: V<sub>t</sub> is the body-biased threshold in V; V<sub>t0</sub> is the zero-bias threshold in V; γ is the body-effect coefficient in V<sup>1/2</sup>; 2φ<sub>F</sub> is the surface potential parameter in V; V<sub>SB</sub> is the source-to-body voltage in V.

blocks.text: A larger V<sub>tn</sub> means a larger drop. The body of the nMOS is tied to ground in a standard n-well process, so this effect is always present when the source node is high.

sections.h3: pMOS pass transistor and transmission gate

blocks.text: A pMOS pass transistor is the dual. It passes a high input well because its source can sit at the high rail and its gate at 0 V keeps V<sub>GS</sub> negative. It passes a low input poorly: the output falls only to |V<sub>tp</sub>| above ground, then the pMOS turns off. So one transistor alone always loses one threshold on one rail.

A transmission gate (TG) fixes this by placing an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel. The nMOS gate is driven by C, the pMOS gate by C bar, the complement of C. When C = 1, both are on and Y = A. When C = 0, both are off and Y is high impedance (high-Z). The pMOS carries the high part of the swing; the nMOS carries the low part. Together they pass the full rail.

The symbol is a switch with two control inputs, one drawn with a bubble for the pMOS. Some syllabi call a network of these switches pass transistor logic (PTL). When complementary data and control signals are used in several branches, some syllabi call it complementary pass-transistor logic. The idea is the same: data travels through switches, not through a complementary CMOS gate.

Transmission gates build useful functions with few transistors. Two TGs form a 2:1 multiplexer: one TG connects A when C = 1, the other connects B when C = 0. An XOR gate uses two TGs and two inverters, or a small TG network, and is common in adder cells. A D flip-flop can use TGs as the input and feedback switches.

PTL saves transistors but has costs. A passed high through an nMOS alone stops at V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>, and a passed low through a pMOS alone stops at |V<sub>tp</sub>| above ground, not at 0 V. So outputs may be weak. Weak nodes are slower and more sensitive to noise. Each stage whose gate is held at V<sub>DD</sub> stops at V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>. Drops pile up only when a later gate or control is itself a passed level, as in some PTL networks. Delay grows with chain length in both cases. If the output drives a gate, a restoring inverter or a full CMOS stage is added at the end. Charge sharing is another issue: when switches change, charge on an internal node can redistribute and disturb the output. Floating nodes must not drive control inputs.

Use PTL where the function is switch-like: multiplexers, XOR/XNOR, adders and flip-flops. Use static CMOS from Chapter 3.7 when full rail restoration and robust noise margins are required. Dynamic logic in Chapter 3.9 also uses clocked switches, but it precharges first.

examples.question: An nMOS pass transistor has V<sub>in</sub> = 3.3 V, gate voltage V<sub>G</sub> = 3.3 V and threshold V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.6 V. (a) Find the maximum output voltage. (b) A transmission gate adds a pMOS in parallel with its gate at 0 V. What maximum output does the transmission gate pass?
steps: For the nMOS passing a high level, the source is the output Y. V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>G</sub> − Y.
The nMOS turns off at V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>tn</sub>. Set V<sub>G</sub> − Y = V<sub>tn</sub>.
Solve: Y = V<sub>G</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub> = 3.3 V − 0.6 V = 2.7 V.
The transmission gate has a pMOS in parallel. Its gate is at 0 V, its source is at 3.3 V, so V<sub>GS</sub> = −3.3 V and the pMOS is on.
The pMOS passes the full high rail, so the TG maximum output is 3.3 V.
examples.answer: The nMOS alone passes a maximum of 2.7 V; the transmission gate passes 3.3 V.
examples.check:
vin = 3.3
vg = 3.3
vtn = 0.6
vout_nmos = vg - vtn
vout_tg = vin
print(round(vout_nmos, 2))
print(round(vout_tg, 2))

traps: Do not use V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> for an nMOS passing a high level. The output stops at V<sub>G</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>, and body effect makes V<sub>tn</sub> larger.
Do not say a pMOS passes a low level perfectly. A pMOS alone stops at |V<sub>tp</sub>| above ground.
Do not confuse a transmission gate with a single pass transistor. The TG has both nMOS and pMOS in parallel and needs C and C bar.
Do not ignore high-Z. When C = 0, a TG output is floating; a following gate must not be left without a defined level.
Do not forget that the pMOS gate is controlled by C bar, not C. Reversing the controls turns both transistors off or makes the switch behave wrongly.

quiz.q: For an nMOS pass transistor with gate at V<sub>DD</sub>, input at V<sub>DD</sub> and threshold V<sub>tn</sub>, what is the maximum output voltage?
quiz.a: V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>. The nMOS turns off when V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>tn</sub>.

quiz.q: In a transmission gate, which control signal drives the pMOS gate?
quiz.a: C bar, the complement of C.

quiz.q: Why does a single pMOS pass transistor fail to pass a full 0 V?
quiz.a: It turns off when its gate-to-source voltage reaches V<sub>tp</sub>, leaving the output at |V<sub>tp</sub>| above ground.

quiz.q: How does body effect change the threshold drop of an nMOS passing a high level?
quiz.a: The source is above ground, so V<sub>SB</sub> > 0. The threshold V<sub>t</sub> rises above V<sub>t0</sub>, so the output V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>t</sub> is lower.

quiz.q: An nMOS pass transistor has V<sub>G</sub> = 2.5 V, V<sub>in</sub> = 2.5 V, V<sub>t0</sub> = 0.5 V. Body effect raises V<sub>t</sub> to 0.7 V. Find the maximum output.
A transmission gate has V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.4 V and |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.4 V. What are the output high and low levels it can pass?
quiz.a: High = 1.8 V through the pMOS; low = 0 V through the nMOS.

quiz.q: A TG output feeds a long wire and then a CMOS gate. Why is a restoring inverter often placed after the TG?
quiz.a: The TG output may be weak or disturbed by charge sharing. The inverter restores full rails and improves noise margin and drive.

quiz.q: Compare a 2:1 multiplexer built from transmission gates with a static CMOS AND-OR-INVERT style mux. Give one advantage and one disadvantage.
quiz.a: A TG 2:1 mux uses about 4 transistors plus one inverter for C bar; a static CMOS mux uses more transistors. The TG output floats (high-Z) when no branch is selected, internal nodes can share charge, and both C and C bar are needed. A TG output is weak only if C or C bar is itself a passed, degraded level. Static CMOS always drives the output to a rail.

beyond: Not for the exam. Transmission gates are common in standard-cell libraries for multiplexers, XOR cells and scan flip-flops. In advanced nodes, finFETs and low-voltage designs make the loss through a single pass transistor worse, so engineers use full transmission gates or restore buffers. EDA tools check charge sharing and floating nodes during simulation. Search for 'transmission gate XOR', 'pass transistor logic standard cell' and 'charge sharing in dynamic logic'.
